titre_video: Why the 2022 Car Bubble is Bursting Now

segments.titre: The auto loan bloodbath: 2.2 million cars repossessed
segments.resume: The video opens with the claim that 2.2 million cars are being taken from their owners, with 1.73 million repossessions in 2024 alone. It presents this as a trap built by auto dealers and predatory lenders, called the great auto loan bloodbath. The lenders who engineered it are said not to realise they will be dragged down with it.
segments.texte: Right now, 2.2 million cars are being ripped away from their owners. People have stumbled into a trap laid by autodealers, a system that was designed to bankrupt them from day 1. This corporate greed saw 1.73 million cars being repossessed in 2024 alone. But this isn’t the result of bad luck. It’s the great auto loan bloodbath. And it isn’t just ordinary Americans suffering. The predatory lenders who engineered it all don’t even realise they’re about to be dragged down with it.

segments.titre: 2022 supply chain collapse and chip shortage
segments.resume: In 2022 the worst of the pandemic was over, but the global supply chain was shattered and key manufacturing hubs stayed locked down. Microchips and other vital components vanished from the market, and vehicle production ground to a halt while industry experts urged patience.
segments.texte: Back in 2022, the automotive industry was being rigged. The worst of the pandemic was over, but the global supply chain was shattered. Faced with long-term disruptions, many countries remained closed for business. With key manufacturing hubs still locked down, vital components like microchips vanished from the market. Vehicle production ground to a halt. Industry experts urged patience, that manufacturing would ramp up eventually.

segments.titre: Soaring demand pushes car prices to a record
segments.resume: After months stuck at home, people had money and demand for cars exploded, including a surge of interest in collector's cars. High demand plus a component shortage drove average auto prices to a record just over $49,500 in 2022. Many buyers could not afford that price, but dealerships were ready to make a deal.
segments.texte: But buyers didn’t want to wait. After months of being stuck at home, people had money. And they wanted to spend it. Demand for cars exploded. It wasn’t just two-doors and station wagons either, there was a huge surge in interest in collector’s cars. The economy is always driven by supply and demand, and 2022 brought a perfect storm. High demand, plus a shortage of components meant prices rose quickly… and kept going. Over the course of the year, auto prices reached an all-time record high of just over $49,500 and many people couldn’t afford the price tag. But that didn’t mean walking away from the dealership empty handed. There’s always a deal to be made.

segments.titre: Molly and the stretched-out car loan
segments.resume: Molly, a 32-year-old teacher in a one-car family with a contractor husband, cannot afford a second car outright and must take an auto loan. Dealerships make the deal painless by lowering the payment through a longer loan duration. If things go south it is the bank's problem, but soon it might be everyone's problem.
segments.texte: Take Molly. She’s 32, married and works as a teacher. It’s a one-car family, her husband needs it for work, and the kids take the school bus. A two-income household used to be a ticket to financial stability, but a teacher and a contractor don’t have the savings needed to buy a second car outright. Especially when rates are high. So, there’s no choice but to take out an auto loan. Dealerships specialize in this, and they know how to make the deal as painless as possible initially. That means driving down the loan payments, usually by extending the duration of the loan. Get them to sign on the dotted line, and things go south, it’s the bank’s problem. But soon, it might be everyone’s problem.

segments.titre: Loan terms creeping toward 84 months
segments.resume: The average car loan lasts about 69 months, nearly six years, but that is becoming the low end as more loans creep toward seven years. Around 23% of the new-car market is in loans of 84 months or longer as of early 2026. These loans keep the monthly payment low, but the interest more than makes up for it by the end.
segments.texte: The average car loan is around 69 months, almost 6 years. But that’s becoming the low end of the deal. More and more loans are creeping towards the 7-year mark. Around a 23% of the new-car market is tied into loans that are 84 months or longer as of early 2026. Generally, this kind of long-term loan is used to encourage people to sign up for a monthly payment on the lower end. However, by the end of the loan, the interest will have more than made up for this. Sometimes, even that’s not a benefit.

segments.titre: Payments over $1,000 a month and Molly signs
segments.resume: In late 2022 only 15.7% of new car buyers had a monthly payment over $1,000, and that share has since crossed 20%. Molly sees a $950 monthly payment, does the math and signs, expecting to pay for a long time as long as the family's situation stays stable. The passage ends by noting that stability is never guaranteed.
segments.texte: As of late 2022, only 15.7% of new car buyers had a monthly payment of over $1,000. However, that number is rising and has crossed the 20% margin since. For Molly, though, she sees the $950 monthly payment, does some math in her head, and signs on the dotted line. She’ll be paying off this car for a long time, but as long as the family’s status quo stays relatively stable, it should be fine. But that’s never a guarantee.

segments.titre: Why lenders don't want to be paid back quickly
segments.resume: Dealerships and banks have already planned for borrowers whose lives are thrown into flux by an unstable world. A dirty little secret of lending is that lenders don't want loans repaid too quickly, because the money and the interest stop once the debt is paid. The ideal borrower eventually pays off the loan but makes minimum payments, padding the lender's margins.
segments.texte: For millions of people, the instability of the world can throw their car plans into flux. But the dealerships and banks have already planned for that. If banks only lent to people who were in good financial positions and could repay loans quickly, they wouldn’t be in business long. One of the dirty little secrets of the lending business is that they don’t want to get paid back too quickly. Once the debt is paid off, the money stops. And so does the interest. The ideal sweet spot for a lender is someone who will be able to pay off the loan at the end of the day, but will make minimum payments. That gives the lender the free money that pads their margins.

segments.titre: Subprime lending and why car loans escaped the stigma
segments.resume: Subprime lending gives loans to riskier borrowers, with poor credit history, missed payments or little collateral, at higher interest rates. The practice got a bad name from the 2007 subprime mortgage crisis and the 2008 recession, and fell out of favor for housing but not for cars. Car loans are a smaller business, a repossession is less severe than losing a home, and defenders say subprime is the only way for people with no debt history to make a big first purchase.
segments.texte: If someone is a risk factor, there’s a plan for that too. Subprime lending is an important element of finance, a system for providing loans to people deemed as more risky. These might be people with a poor credit history, some missed payments for a past loan, or a lack of suitable collateral. But that doesn’t stop the banks. These loans will usually feature higher interest rates as compensation for the increased risk of default. The practice got a very bad name due to the subprime mortgage crisis of 2007, setting the stage for the 2008 recession that destroyed the global economy. The practice has fallen out of favor for housing… But not for cars. Car loans are a smaller business for everyone involved. If a banker sees defaults on car loans, it’s not going to have as much of an impact on their bottom loan. A repossessed car is a tough blow, but it’s not like losing your home. And there are ways to get a car for cheaper, allowing someone to get a subprime loan for a used or refurbished car. Defenders of subprime loans say it’s the only way people with limited or no debt experience will be able to make a big purchase for the first time. For some, it can feel like a lifeline.

segments.titre: Tom, a first-time buyer, signs a 19% subprime loan
segments.resume: Tom, 28, a diner cook with a brief jail stint behind him, wants to drive for Uber but has no car and no credit history. A used-car dealer offers a certified pre-owned two-door with 14,000 miles on a 72-month loan at $600 a month and a 19% interest rate, typical for subprime. Excited about a fresh start, he ignores the rate, which is exactly what the banks are counting on.
segments.texte: Meet Tom. He’s 28, and after a brief stint in jail for being drunk and disorderly, he’s gotten things together. He has 2 roommates in a 7th-floor apartment, and was holding down a job as a cook at the local diner. He was looking for a new job when his roommate told him about how much money he makes driving for Uber. There’s just one problem. Tom needs a car. Growing up in a city where public transportation was second nature, he never needed one. He’s never owned a house, and he did two semesters of community college with no student loans. That means no real credit history. So, he’s not optimistic when he walks into the used-car dealership for the first time. But the dealer has Tom’s best interests at heart and soon, he’s offered a certified pre-owned two-door with 14,000 miles (22,530 km) on it. Suddenly car ownership sounds possible. The loan will last 72 months and the payments are $600. Tom is won over by the terms and signs up. Now he just needs to keep things together: start driving for Uber as soon as possible, make monthly payments on time, and keep himself on the straight and narrow. As a first-time car owner, he doesn’t pay much attention to the 19% interest rate, a typical number for a subprime loan. He’s just too excited to kick off his new life. That’s exactly what the banks are counting on.

segments.titre: 108 million auto loans and $350 billion in subprime debt
segments.resume: As of 2026 there are over 108 million active auto loans in the United States, totaling over $1.7 trillion and held by about 86 million people. Over 20% are subprime, with up to 19 million active subprime loans holding over $350 billion in debt. Banks assume some will default and can recoup their losses, so it is all baked in, but it may soon come home to roost.
segments.texte: Across the United States, there are over 108 million auto loans active as of 2026, totaling over $1.7 trillion. Those loans are held by approximately 86 million people. That’s over a quarter of the United States. And of those loans, over 20% of those are subprime loans, with up to 19 million active subprime loans holding over $350 billion in debt. At those numbers, the banks are assuming that some of them are going to default. When they do, they’ll simply be able to recoup their losses when the loans go bust. It’s all baked in. And it may be coming home to roost soon.

segments.titre: Loans taken out of necessity and the collector car illusion
segments.resume: Many loans were taken out of necessity after car values skyrocketed and priced people out, while others bet on cars as a long-term asset whose value would only rise. That thinking was at the heart of the collector's car market, where prices shot up amid post-pandemic impulse buys. Those numbers turned out to be an illusion that is quickly fading away.
segments.texte: The loans were largely taken out of necessity, as the result of a disastrous market that saw the value of cars skyrocket. People found themselves priced out of a necessity, and did what they had to in order to keep going. Others took a swing on what they thought was a good long-term asset, assuming that the value would only keep going up. That thinking was at the heart of the collector’s car market during this period. Prices shot up amid a surge of impulse buys in the aftermath of the pandemic. But those numbers turned out to be an illusion. One that’s quickly fading away.

segments.titre: Herman buys a $55,000 Corvette for retirement
segments.resume: Herman, 61, an account manager near retirement, buys a restored 1971 Corvette priced at over $55,000. With good credit and a golf connection to the bank president, he is approved for a little over $1,000 a month over 60 months at around 12% interest. Molly, Tom and Herman, a practical buyer, a fresh start and a splurge, are more alike than they realise.
segments.texte: At 61, Herman’s is approaching his golden years. His kids are at college, he’s still on friendly terms with his ex-wife and he’s built up a good nest egg from his years as an account manager at an investment firm. With retirement on the horizon, he has big plans. Number 1 on the bucket list is hitting the open road. And he wants to do it in style. As soon as he walks into the collector’s car dealership, he’s won over by the 1971 Corvette, lovingly restored and in driving condition. Sure, the price tag of over $55,000 is intimidating, but he has good credit and he’s going to get an auto loan with ease. The bank very quickly approves his deal. It’s not really a surprise, he’s played golf with the bank President a number of times. He’ll be paying a little over $1,000 a month on a 60-month loan, with an interest rate of around 12%. It’ll be mostly paid off by the time he retires, and until then, that car is going to look pretty impressive parked in his driveway. Molly, Tom, and Herman couldn’t be more different. One is making a practical decision. One is trying for a fresh start. And one is making a dramatic splurge. But they’re more alike than they realise.

segments.titre: Delinquencies rise from 4% to 5%
segments.resume: The car market bubble has burst, but prices haven't gone down. Auto loan delinquencies, defined as over 90 days overdue, were about 4% at the end of 2022 and ticked up to 5% by the end of 2024. Stagnant wages and rising costs like groceries lock more people into loans they can't afford.
segments.texte: Over the last few years, something terrible has happened to the car market in the United States. The bubble has burst, but the prices haven’t gone down. At the end of 2022, approximately 4% of auto loans were delinquent, defined as being over 90 days overdue as of the latest payment. But as of the end of 2024, that number had ticked up to 5%. As wages stay stagnant and the cost of daily expenses like groceries continues to rise, more people are being locked into loans that they can’t afford. And time runs out sooner than most people think.

segments.titre: 1.73 million repossessions: the worst since 2009
segments.resume: The speech pictures a bumper-to-bumper line of cars from New York to Los Angeles and back to illustrate the 1.73 million cars repossessed in 2024. That is the worst repossession number since 2009, the peak of the Great Recession, and the numbers keep getting worse.
segments.texte: Imagine the worst traffic jam you’ve ever seen, an endless line of cars forming a bumper-to-bumper caravan stretching from New York all the way to Los Angeles. Then, when you turn around, the exact same line is stretching all the way across the country back to the starting position. That’s what 1.73 million cars would look like, and that’s the number that was repossessed in 2024 alone. It’s the worst number of repossessions since 2009, the peak of the Great Recession. And across the line, the numbers keep on getting worse.

segments.titre: Molly surrenders her car voluntarily
segments.resume: Molly's car seemed a practical move, but her husband's contracting work slowed, his work truck needed costly repairs and her raise was lost to district budget cuts. The second car became deadweight, so they arranged a voluntary surrender with the bank. Because they had paid faithfully for years, the sale covered the remaining balance and they owed nothing, though their credit score was damaged.
segments.texte: For Molly, getting a new car seemed to be a good idea. It was a practical move designed to get her to and from work faster, and give her more time at home each day. Her family’s financial status seemed stable. The loan seemed manageable. But reality had other plans. It wasn’t long before one minor factor after another started cropping up. Her husband’s work started slowing down as the flagging economy meant fewer people had money for home improvements. Then his work truck had engine trouble, which meant costly repairs that thankfully were more affordable than having to get a new truck. And her hopes of a raise were dashed due to district budget cuts. Suddenly, a second car looked more and more like a deadweight rather than a necessity. Facing the risk of defaulting on their loan and having the car repossessed, Molly and her husband arranged for a voluntary surrender with the bank. The car was taken into the bank’s custody, to be sold as a pre-owned vehicle. Because they had been faithfully paying off the loan for the last few years, the sale covered the remaining balance. They didn’t owe any further money. It damaged their credit score, but they were no longer in debt and able to move forward.

segments.titre: Prime vs subprime defaults: subprime hits a 32-year high
segments.resume: Molly and her husband were moderate-risk borrowers in the vast minority who default; there is no epidemic of prime borrowers with 750 credit scores surrendering cars, and prime delinquency remains under 1%. The growing crisis comes from subprime borrowers defaulting, with numbers at a 32-year high. Many pay over $1,000 a month, which equals the median monthly rent in 15 lower-cost US states.
segments.texte: But not everyone is so lucky. Molly and her husband were standard borrowers, seen as moderate risk, but they didn’t manage to keep up with the payment due to outside factors. They’re in the vast minority of borrowers who default on their loans. There is no epidemic of prime borrowers with 750 credit scores surrendering cars, and prime delinquency remains under 1%. The source of the growing crisis is the large number of subprime borrowers defaulting, as the numbers hit a 32-year high. Many people are paying over $1,000 in monthly payments, which is the median monthly rent in 15 lower-cost US states. For subprime borrowers, it often doesn’t take long for things to go wrong.

segments.titre: Tom's Uber income collapses and his car is repossessed
segments.resume: Tom earns well with Uber at peak times, but the income is unreliable and swings with events and weather. A passenger's false report locks his account for two weeks, he misses a payment, more rideshare competition arrives and more payments are missed. A tow truck takes his car at 6:30 in the morning, the repossession hits his credit score, and he goes back to working at the diner.
segments.texte: Things were looking up for Tom. His friend was right, if you knew the right times and places, Uber was a great money-maker. But it also wasn’t reliable. The numbers could dry up at any time, and it became a game of feast and famine. When the local basketball team was in the playoffs, he was racking up hundreds every night. But when a nasty cold snap hit the city and tourism dried up, he was scraping dollars together. He was barely making his monthly car payments every month. Then, disaster struck. A customer didn’t like to be told not to vape in the car, so he filed a false report against Tom on the Uber platform. Under Uber’s policies, that meant Tom’s account was locked while they investigated, and he couldn’t take any rides. Fortunately, he had good enough documentation to get his account restored, but he lost 2 weeks of income. He wasn’t able to make his payment for one month, and had that hanging over his head. Things didn’t get better from there. More and more rideshare accounts signed up for the service, providing more competition for Tom. The tourist season was slow. More payments were missed. One day, he woke up to an unpleasant surprise. A tow truck, at 6:30 in the morning, was dragging his vehicle away. He ran downstairs, thinking his car was being stolen, but the bank had everything in order. The car would be going to its third owner in short order, and Tom’s lifeline to drive for Uber was gone in a flash. The repossession would be on his credit score and make it very hard to get a loan for another car, and his savings account was mostly tapped out. Soon, he was back working as a chef in the diner. It was another failed loan.

segments.titre: Trade-ins: the dealership appraisal sets the value
segments.resume: For borrowers who don't default but want to unload a car, the most common route is a trade-in: the dealership appraises the car for refurbishment and resale and takes that value off a new purchase. But the value depends on the dealership's review, and trade-in values are only getting worse.
segments.texte: But that’s not the worst of the problems for some. For most people who don’t default on their car loans but want to unload the car, the most common route is a trade-in. They’ll take their car to a dealership, get it appraised for refurbishment and resale, and get a new car. It’s a great way to lose a car that no longer suits your needs and take that value off the purchase of a new car. But that value depends on the dealership’s review. And those values are only getting worse.

segments.titre: Negative equity: owing more than the car is worth
segments.resume: Millions of people have negative equity, meaning the car is worth less than the remaining balance on the loan. When they surrender the car or trade it in, the balance doesn't go away; they must pay it off or roll it into a new loan if they can get one. That means heavier monthly payments and more interest, keeping people locked in debt.
segments.texte: Millions of people have found themselves in a nasty financial trap. They have negative equity on their cars, where the value of the car is lower than the remaining balance on their car loan. When they surrender the vehicle or trade it in, the balance doesn’t go away. They get the value of the car taken off, but then they have to pay off the remaining balance or refinance it into a new car loan… if they can get one. That means heavier monthly payments and more interest, keeping people locked in a trap of debt. That can take the shine off a new car soon.

segments.titre: Herman's Corvette loses value and he pays to leave
segments.resume: Herman's Corvette was a talking point at first, but a bad back and a new interest in cruises made the vintage car a liability as retirement approached. Its value had dropped since the collectible market peak, and with the loan interest he still owed several thousand dollars after the trade-in, so he cut a check. The speech notes he is far from alone.
segments.texte: For Herman, his new Corvette was a great talking point for the first few years. But as his retirement party approached, his age started catching up to him. He had thrown out his back a year ago, leading to months of physical therapy and a nagging problem with sitting for long periods. That made the idea of a road trip less and less appealing. Besides, he had met a pretty widow a few months back, and she was more interested in spending retirement on a cruise ship than on Route 66. Slowly, that vintage car hanging around his driveway started looking more like a liability and he thought it might be time to cut bait. But he was in for a nasty surprise. Herman had done everything right, but the value of the car had declined significantly since it was purchased at the height of the collectible car market. That, combined with the interest on the loan, meant he would still owe several thousand dollars after the trade-in. Frustrated, he cut a check and waved goodbye to the costly car. Herman is far from alone.

segments.titre: Average negative equity on trade-ins nears $6,900
segments.resume: As of 2023 the average negative equity on car loan trade-ins was over $6,000, and it climbed to almost $6,900 by mid-2026. People are in debt and the numbers are getting worse even when they surrender their cars, and the speech says it is all by design.
segments.texte: As of 2023, the average negative equity for car loan trade-ins was over $6,000, but it had climbed to almost $6,900 by mid-2026. People are in debt and the numbers are getting worse, even when they surrender the cars. And it’s all by design.

segments.titre: A microcosm of 2008: the 84-month loans of the 2022 bubble
segments.resume: The speech argues the crisis is not only the result of the economy's struggles but a microcosm of the 2008 collapse, when people couldn't pay subprime mortgages. In 2022, as the car market hit a bubble, lenders offered a wave of 84-month loans designed for slow payoff with small monthly payments, which appealed to subprime borrowers and hid the true cost of the car. The bill has now come due.
segments.texte: Looking at the crisis right now, it’s easy to assume it’s all the result of the economy’s ongoing struggles. But really, what’s happening right now is a microcosm of the 2008 economic collapse, where people were unable to pay off subprime mortgages on their houses. In 2022, as the car market hit a bubble, lenders offered a wave of 84-month loans that were designed to be paid off slowly with smaller monthly payments. This made them appealing to struggling or subprime borrowers, and hid the true cost of the car. But the bill has come due.

segments.titre: The trap: banks and dealerships win, drivers lose
segments.resume: This might be what the banks wanted: a trap many buyers can't escape. Borrowers pay off part of the loan, including interest, and then the car goes right back where it came from. The banks and dealerships win while the drivers lose.
segments.texte: This might be what the banks wanted. They laid a trap that many buyers can’t escape. They pay off part of the loan, including interest, and then send the car right back where it came from. The banks and dealerships win, the drivers lose.

segments.titre: Ghost cars, inventory glut and the bubble about to pop
segments.resume: Soon no one will be winning: millions of drivers are driving ghost cars, paying off a value based on an economy that no longer exists. As more cars are repossessed or traded in, the glut of inventory lowers values further in a vicious cycle. When dealerships can't sell them, the car bubble won't just deflate but pop, possibly taking banks and businesses down with it.
segments.texte: Except that soon, no one will be winning. Millions of drivers are driving ghost cars, paying off value based on an economy that no longer exists as the value of the car declines. And as more and more cars get repossessed or traded in, the glut of inventory continues. And that will lower the value even more. It’s a vicious cycle. Drivers can’t afford cars, but what happens when the dealerships can’t sell them? As the unprecedented surge in repossessions increases, the car bubble isn’t just going to deflate. It’s going to pop. And it could take banks and businesses down with it.

segments.titre: Auto industry crisis and the Ford teaser
segments.resume: The auto industry is staring down the barrel of a crisis, and every manufacturer is feeling the heat. One Detroit powerhouse is beginning to panic, and viewers are pointed to another video titled REAL Reason Why FORD Is Failing.
mots_cles: REAL Reason Why FORD Is Failing
segments.texte: The auto industry is staring down the barrel of a crisis. But while every manufacturer is feeling the heat, one Detroit powerhouse is beginning to panic. e. Watch “REAL Reason Why FORD Is Failing” to find out why. Or click on this.
